title: October 1 Readiness: The Last Operational Checks Revenue Cycle Leaders Should Make
summary: A practical 48-hour October 1 readiness checklist for Revenue Cycle leaders covering system updates, payer requirements, workflows, chargemaster changes, claim edits, testing, training, mitigation, and go/no-go validation.
body_markdown:
By the time October 1 arrives, Revenue Cycle leaders should not still be asking whether the work was assigned.


The question should be whether the changes were actually implemented, tested, communicated, and validated.


Every year, October 1 brings changes that can affect coding, reimbursement, payer requirements, authorization workflows, system logic, claim edits, and operational processes.


Most organizations know these changes are coming.


The bigger risk is assuming readiness because each department says its work is “in progress.”


For me, final readiness comes down to one thing:


**Can we prove that the changes are in place and that the organization is ready to operate under them?**


## Readiness Workstreams Should Move at the Same Time


I would not look at October 1 readiness as a sequential checklist.


These workstreams should be moving in parallel:


- system updates,
- payer requirement review,
- workflow review and updates,
- chargemaster changes,
- claim edits,
- testing,
- staff training,
- communication,
- and overall readiness validation.


Each area has its own work, but they are connected.


A system change can affect a workflow. A payer requirement can change an authorization process. A chargemaster update can affect claim edits. A workflow can look correct on paper and still fail once it reaches Billing.


That is why the organization needs visibility across all of the workstreams at the same time.


## Start With System Updates


The first thing I would want confirmed is that required system updates are complete.


Not requested. Not assigned. Not scheduled. Complete.


That includes confirming that the changes are live in the correct environment and that downstream functionality has been validated.


A system update should not be considered finished simply because someone says the build was completed.


The real question is:


**Did the change work the way it was supposed to work?**


That validation is what turns a technical task into operational readiness.


## Review Payer Requirements Before They Become Denials


Payer requirements also need to be reviewed before October 1.


Organizations should confirm whether any changes affect prior authorization, notification requirements, coding, medical necessity, billing rules, claim submission, documentation, or payer-specific edits.


If a requirement changed, the operational workflow should change with it.


It is not enough for one department to receive a payer update. The people doing the work need to know what changed and what they are expected to do differently.


## Re-Review the Workflow, Even If It Already Exists


Every impacted workflow should be re-reviewed.


The purpose is not to redesign everything. The purpose is to make sure the current workflow still works after the October 1 changes are applied.


If a workflow needs to change, update it. If ownership changes, document it. If a new handoff is required, define it. If an exception path is needed, build it before go-live.


One of the easiest ways for organizations to create downstream issues is to update the system but leave the old workflow in place.


The system and the operational process have to match.


## Chargemaster Changes Need to Be Loaded and Validated


If chargemaster updates are required, I would want confirmation that the changes are **completed, implemented, loaded into the system, and validated.**


This is another area where “done” can mean different things to different teams.


A spreadsheet being updated does not mean the change is operational.


Revenue Cycle leaders need to know that the correct information is actually in the production environment and behaving as expected.


## Claim Edits and Testing Cannot Be the Last-Minute Step


Testing should not be treated as the final box someone checks after every other task is complete.


It should be happening throughout readiness work.


Claim edits should be reviewed. Test claims should be run. Expected results should be compared to actual results.


And where possible, testing should follow the transaction from the beginning of the workflow through claim generation.


I strongly recommend **end-to-end testing** , not just departmental testing.


A process may work perfectly inside Coding or Patient Access and still fail when it reaches the claim. That is why downstream validation matters.


## Training and Communication Are Part of Readiness


Training and staff communication are not separate from implementation. They are part of it.


If the system changed but the staff does not know what changed, the organization is not ready.


If the workflow changed but the team is still following the old process, the organization is not ready.


Before October 1, affected staff should understand what changed, when it becomes effective, what they need to do differently, where to find the updated workflow, and who to contact if something does not work as expected.


## One Person Should Coordinate Overall Readiness


Whenever possible, I recommend having one operational project lead or project manager coordinate the overall readiness effort.


That person does not replace departmental ownership. Each department is still accountable for its own work.


The project lead’s role is to make sure the workstreams come together, including owners, deadlines, dependencies, open risks, testing status, and final validation.


A centralized readiness tracker can make a significant difference here.


## Hold a Cross-Functional Readiness Review


In the final week before October 1, I would bring the key stakeholders from each impacted area together for a formal readiness review.


That may include leaders or subject matter experts from Patient Access, Utilization Management, Coding, Clinical Documentation, Revenue Integrity, IT, Billing, Managed Care, and any other area affected by the changes.


If the organization has a project lead, that person should coordinate the meeting.


The meeting should answer three questions:


- **What is complete and validated?**
- **What is still open or at risk?**
- **Who owns the next action and by when?**


## Make the Go/No-Go Decision Two Days Before October 1


I recommend holding a formal **go/no-go review two days before October 1** .


That timing matters. If the meeting happens on September 30, the organization may identify a major issue with no time left to correct it.


Two days before go-live gives the team a final window to resolve remaining gaps.


## Mitigation Should Be Planned Before Go-Live


There may be situations where a critical update will not be completed by the expected timeline.


That is when mitigation planning becomes important.


If a critical system update, claim edit, chargemaster load, or required test will not be complete in time, the organization should have a documented mitigation plan.


In some cases, that may mean placing the **specific impacted claims** on a temporary hold.


But that should be a contingency, not the standard process.


**The goal is not to slow billing down. The goal is to prevent a known readiness gap from creating avoidable downstream errors.**


## 48-Hour Go-Live Readiness Checklist


**Two days before October 1, Revenue Cycle leaders should be able to answer yes to each of these questions:**


- **System updates:** Are all required system changes complete, live, and validated?
- **Payer requirements:** Have payer-specific changes been reviewed and incorporated into operational workflows?
- **Workflow updates:** Have all impacted workflows been re-reviewed and updated where necessary?
- **Chargemaster:** Are all required chargemaster changes completed, loaded, and validated in the system?
- **Claim edits:** Have new or revised claim edits been built and tested?
- **End-to-end testing:** Have test claims been run through the full workflow and produced the expected result?
- **Training:** Have impacted staff been trained on what is changing and what they need to do differently?
- **Communication:** Has the final communication gone out to all affected teams?
- **Ownership:** Does every remaining open item have a named owner and deadline?
- **Risk review:** Are there any unresolved issues that could affect claims, authorization, coding, reimbursement, or billing?
- **Mitigation:** If an item will not be complete by October 1, is there a documented mitigation plan?
- **Claim hold contingency:** If needed, has the organization identified exactly which impacted claims or services should be held until the issue is corrected and validated?
- **Escalation path:** Do staff know who to contact if something fails after go-live?
- **Leadership signoff:** Has the cross-functional group completed the final go/no-go review?


**If October 1 were tomorrow, would we be comfortable allowing these claims to move through the system?**


If the answer is no, the organization still has work to do.


## October 1 Readiness Is Really About Validation


The final days before October 1 are not the time for assumptions. They are the time for validation.


Did the system update actually go live? Were payer requirements translated into the workflow? Were chargemaster changes loaded? Did the claim edit behave as expected? Did the test claim pass? Did staff receive the training? Do they know what changed?


And if something is still not ready, does the organization have a mitigation plan?


Because readiness is not about how much work was completed.


**It is about whether the organization is prepared to operate correctly when October 1 arrives.**
